concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: computer
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a computer or processing device is used in a broad sense to mean a device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the world.

concepts.name: display
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a display or output device is used in a broad sense to mean any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not only a visual display.
A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

concepts.name: marker
concepts.definition: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.

defining_facts.text: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.
Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.
Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications are easier to build but difficult to maintain because markers are prone to damage, and a damaged marker may make the application not work.

Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.

concepts.name: global positioning system
concepts.definition: Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).

defining_facts.text: Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).
The global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device that is particularly useful in outdoor environments.
The global positioning system (GPS) generally offers low accuracy, particularly in indoor environments, and allows only positional tracking.

Real time kinematic (RTK) technology can be used with a basic global positioning system (GPS) sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement, providing further accuracy than the basic global positioning system.

The global positioning system (GPS) is typically utilized when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid tracking system with other tracking systems.

concepts.name: sensor
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.
Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.

The term sensor has two related but structurally different meanings: in a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit; in the human body, human bodily sensors are body organs that convert a stimulus into neural impulses.

concepts.name: field of view
concepts.definition: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.

defining_facts.text: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.
Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).

An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
Field of view (FOV) is the amount of virtual environment that is visible at any moment.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts.

A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience.
A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.
A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.
Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

concepts.name: tracking
concepts.definition: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

defining_facts.text: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.
Tracking is an integral hardware component of an extended reality (XR) system.
Keeping track of motion in the physical world is a crucial part of any extended reality (XR) system, more importantly in virtual reality (VR) systems.
In virtual reality (VR), tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so that it can be translated into virtual motion in the virtual world.

In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view.
Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.
There are two broad ways to obtain input for tracking: inside-out and outside-in.
The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.
In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.

In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

Low-level libraries and frameworks are the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.

ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.
ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library: it provides functions that enable a developer to perform tracking and then carry out a related activity.

Many standard augmented reality (AR) toolkits or low-level libraries primarily provide tracking support but lack the features needed for realistic rendering of digital content over the real-world view and for interaction support.

To overcome the limitations of ARToolKit or other tracking-focused low-level libraries, a framework for augmented reality (AR) system development can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support.

When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.

In an augmented reality (AR) example in which a phone detects a marker on a table and a three-dimensional (3D) cow object appears on the screen, the operation involves tracking, which recognizes the marker and its position, and three-dimensional (3D) registration, which creates and renders the cow at that position.

In the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph (OSG) or Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) can perform the operations: ARToolKit handles tracking and three-dimensional (3D) registration, while OSG handles creation of the AR scene with the rendered cow.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.

Examples of frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries include the Open Scene Graph (OSG) ART 3 library, which links ARToolKit for tracking support with OSG for real-time rendering features; Goblin XNA, which combines the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform; and Metaio SDK plus OSG, in which the Metaio SDK provides augmented reality (AR) tracking technologies and OSG provides rendering support.

Mobile-specific augmented reality (AR) frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia; DroidAR uses other sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support.

concepts.name: three-dimensional registration
concepts.definition: In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

defining_facts.text: In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

In 1997, wearable computers with global positioning system (GPS) tracking produced outdoor augmented reality (AR) interfaces that showed information in place in the real world, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.
Viewpoint tracking was one of the most significant challenges of augmented reality (AR), and it was addressed so that three-dimensional registration of content could happen accurately.

Three-dimensional (3D) registration in augmented reality (AR) means anchoring virtual content in the real world at a suitable place so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.

To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

In an augmented reality (AR) example in which a phone detects a marker on a table and a three-dimensional (3D) cow object appears on the screen, the operation involves tracking, which recognizes the marker and its position, and three-dimensional (3D) registration, which creates and renders the cow at that position.

In the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph (OSG) or Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) can perform the operations: ARToolKit handles tracking and three-dimensional (3D) registration, while OSG handles creation of the AR scene with the rendered cow.

concepts.name: AR Toolkit
concepts.definition: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

defining_facts.text: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.
ARToolKit is one of the most widely adopted software libraries for developing augmented reality (AR) applications; it is written in C and supports platforms such as Windows, Linux, and macOS.

ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.
ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library: it provides functions that enable a developer to perform tracking and then carry out a related activity.

ARToolKit provides only low-level OpenGL-based rendering support, with very primitive rendering and no built-in support for interaction techniques or complex realistic graphics, so using it alone yields a rudimentary system in which the developer must write interaction from scratch, making a complete realistic augmented reality (AR) application difficult and time-consuming.

To overcome the limitations of ARToolKit or other tracking-focused low-level libraries, a framework for augmented reality (AR) system development can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support.

When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.

In the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph (OSG) or Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) can perform the operations: ARToolKit handles tracking and three-dimensional (3D) registration, while OSG handles creation of the AR scene with the rendered cow.

Examples of frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries include the Open Scene Graph (OSG) ART 3 library, which links ARToolKit for tracking support with OSG for real-time rendering features; Goblin XNA, which combines the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform; and Metaio SDK plus OSG, in which the Metaio SDK provides augmented reality (AR) tracking technologies and OSG provides rendering support.

Mobile-specific augmented reality (AR) frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia; DroidAR uses other sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support.
ARToolKit for mobile is a version of ARToolKit available for mobile platforms including iOS and Android, integrated with Open Scene Graph (OSG) but developed for mobile.

concepts.name: rendering
concepts.definition: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

defining_facts.text: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses.

From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

concepts.name: platform
concepts.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

defining_facts.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.
In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.

A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

concepts.name: authoring tool
concepts.definition: An authoring tool for a game engine lets a developer access the different functionalities supported by the game engine in order to develop their own software that runs on top of the game engine.

defining_facts.text: An authoring tool for a game engine lets a developer access the different functionalities supported by the game engine in order to develop their own software that runs on top of the game engine.

An authoring tool for a game engine may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, and its logic setting can sometimes be done through scripting, which can be part of a game engine development environment.

never_defined.name: virtual object
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: augmented reality application
never_defined.definition: In healthcare, augmented reality (AR) applications include medical training, telemedicine options that enable medical professionals to interact with patients, and real-time information to treatment areas that supports diagnosis, surgery, and treatment plans.

never_defined.name: computer vision
never_defined.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques rely primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors, such as global positioning system (GPS) sensors, in location-based applications.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional object
never_defined.definition: Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience.

never_defined.name: web browser
never_defined.definition: The main factors behind the move of augmented reality (AR) from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology in 2009 were Adobe Flash-based AR authoring tools that made experiencing AR through web browsers possible from 2008, smartphone-based AR because the era of smartphones had begun by then, and the use of AR in global marketing campaigns to increase sales and make products popular.

never_defined.name: camera
never_defined.definition: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

never_defined.name: tracking technology
never_defined.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

never_defined.name: link
never_defined.definition: Electromechanical trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

never_defined.name: software library
never_defined.definition: Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.

never_defined.name: physics
never_defined.definition: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

never_defined.name: Mac OS
never_defined.definition: In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.

never_defined.name: Android

never_defined.name: computer graphics scene
never_defined.definition: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

never_defined.name: state management
never_defined.definition: Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.

never_defined.name: C++
